newsitem.title: IRAQ: Red Cross asks for $10 mln for malnourished Iraqis.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross asks for $10 mln for malnourished Iraqis.

text.p: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies has appealed for $10 million to help some 50,000 malnourished Iraqi children and their families because of delays in the arrival of food under a U.N. plan, an aid official said on Thursday.

Iraq resumed partial oil sales in December under Security Council resolution 986 known as the oil-for-food formula, but no food or medicine has yet reached the country. The plan covers the export of oil worth $2 billion in six months.

"Information from the U.N. gave us the impression implementation would start in February or March and now it looks like it might even be April or a bit later," Anthony Ronald Maryon, head of the federation's regional delegation, told reporters in Baghdad.

He said the federation would treat some 50,000 malnourished children, hand out food rations to their families and distribute medical supplies to 22 hospitals "as long as possible until we are sure that 986 is in the (Iraqi) villages and towns".
Iraq has been under stringent economic sanctions imposed by the United Nations after it ivaded Kuwait in 1990.
The appeal, a copy of which was handed to reporters, said prices in Iraq had risen by 50-100 percent in the last quarter of 1996 while wages were not adjusted for inflation.
It said over 80 per cent of Iraq's more than 20 million people had no income in real terms with the average monthly salary of civil servants hovering around $3, the price of one chicken in Baghdad.
Basic services such as sanitation and water supplies were failing, it said, and shortages of medical supplies forced hospitals to function at only 30 percent of capacity.
U.N. sources in Baghdad say first shipments of wheat are expected to reach Iraq in early April and it will take more time for other supplies like sugar and rice to arrive.
Maryon said the federation expected it would take three more months before food reached people and even longer before medical supplies became available.
He said initial response to the appeal, made jointly with Iraq's Red Crescent Society, was encouraging. Fifty percent of the supplies were on their way to Iraq.

Each family covered by the federation receives 18 kg (40 lb) of rice, six kg (13 lb) of lentils and three kg (7 lb) of cooking oil a month and hospitals are provided with their most essential medical supplies and drugs.
